title: Follow One Pot From Centering to Its Final Firing
description: Learn how a wheel-thrown pot moves through centering, shaping, trimming, drying, glazing, and firing under a studio’s kiln schedule.
intent: Explains the full studio path from clay on the wheel to a fired pot, so a beginner can choose a class and understand what happens between sessions.

sections.heading: Pick a form that teaches the wheel
paragraphs: Choose a small cylinder or bowl rather than a tall, thin vase. A short form lets you focus on centering the clay, opening the middle, and pulling the walls without also managing height. Tell the instructor what you hope to make; a teacher can help adjust the target to the clay body, the class length, and the studio’s firing process.

At the wheel, treat the first attempt as a sequence of skills, not a beauty contest. Ceramic educator Kara Leigh Ford recommends bracing the arms, positioning the body close to the wheel, and moving steadily with the clay. Ask the instructor to demonstrate how to keep the base even before you concentrate on a finished profile.

sections.heading: Let the clay firm up before trimming
paragraphs: Once the piece is thrown, it needs to become firm enough to handle. The studio may cover it and set it aside until the clay reaches a stage suitable for trimming the foot. This pause is part of the craft: trim too early and the form can distort; wait too long and the clay may be difficult to cut cleanly. Follow the teacher’s guidance for your studio’s clay and room conditions.

At trimming, identify which surface will meet the table and how much foot is needed to support the form. A bowl often benefits from a stable base rather than a narrow, delicate ring. If the piece looks uneven, ask whether trimming can correct it or whether that unevenness belongs to the shape. Do not cut away material just to imitate a reference image.

sections.heading: Drying and first firing set the next limits
paragraphs: Clay must dry sufficiently before firing. A studio may dry pieces slowly to reduce uneven shrinkage; the exact timing depends on the form, clay, and conditions. Avoid taking a damp piece away to dry at home unless the instructor explicitly says to. Keep your project labeled, and check how the studio will notify you when the first firing is complete.

A first firing changes soft clay into a durable but still porous ceramic body. It is a studio operation, not a home experiment: ask the teacher what the studio’s process means for later decoration and glaze choice. Your part is to make the form and follow instructions about what materials may go on it before firing.

sections.heading: Choose glaze for the object’s shape
paragraphs: Before glazing, inspect the form and decide where you want color to gather. A rim band, interior pool, or two-color overlap can make a simple silhouette expressive. Ask how many coats, which surfaces must stay clear, and how to prevent glaze from sticking the pot to the kiln shelf. Studios use different glazes and firing schedules, so follow the studio’s specific directions rather than copying a recipe online.

Keep the foot and the surface touching the kiln shelf clean as instructed. If you want to test a combination, use a studio-approved test tile rather than gambling the whole pot. Write the glaze names or codes on your tracking card so you can compare the result later and repeat the choice if it works.

sections.heading: Make the finished piece useful to you
paragraphs: After the glaze firing, examine the piece from above and at eye level. Does it sit flat? Is the rim comfortable? Is the glaze what you expected? Small irregularities can make a handmade object distinctive, but sharp edges or structural cracks should be discussed with the studio before you use it. Ask whether its clay and glaze are suitable for the intended use; appearance alone does not answer that question.

Your next action is to book a class that explains trimming, glazing, and collection as clearly as throwing. Ask how many studio visits are involved and what makes a finished piece ready for pickup. Taking home one modest pot whose making you understand is a stronger beginning than producing several forms without knowing how they become ceramic.
